passage: I'm Afreen, Zubin's older sister, and for three months I've watched my brother run a quiet experiment. He works in accounts at a logistics firm and keeps saying he admires people who build furniture. He didn't quit. First he signed up for a Saturday carpentry workshop at the polytechnic, eight weeks, fees less than his phone bill. Then he emailed a woman who runs a small furniture studio in Bandra and asked if he could watch her team for one afternoon. She said yes. He came home with sawdust in his hair and a page of questions. Last week he made a bedside stool; one leg is shorter, and he laughed about it. I can't tell if he'll switch careers. I only know he talks about wood the way he used to talk about cricket, and his office badge still hangs by the door.

qa.q: What did Zubin make last week?
qa.a: A bedside stool; one leg is shorter.

qa.q: What does the way Zubin talks about wood suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests real excitement, the same eager interest he once had for cricket.

qa.q: Why are the workshop and the studio visit good steps for Zubin at this stage?
qa.a: They are cheap tests that give him real feedback on carpentry while he keeps his accounts job, so nothing is burned behind him.

qa.q: How does Afreen see her brother's experiment?
qa.a: Afreen notices his new energy and sawdust-covered joy but admits she can't tell where it will lead; she watches with curiosity rather than worry.

grounding: Shows small, low-cost experiments such as a weekend course and a visit to someone doing admired work, giving feedback without quitting.

passage:
Monday, 11 p.m. Vasudha closed the bank spreadsheet and opened a video-editing tutorial for the third night running. She had admired documentary editors since college, but switching careers felt like jumping off a roof.
Saturday. She sat across from Parul, a friend of a friend who edited short films, in a small cafe in Indiranagar. 'What's the boring part nobody mentions?' Vasudha asked. Parul laughed. 'Logging footage. Hours of it.' Vasudha wrote that down. Before the bill came, Parul offered her a small practice task: cut a two-minute trailer from raw clips.
Three weeks later. The trailer was done, rough but real. Parul's notes were blunt: pacing good, sound messy. Vasudha felt stung and oddly thrilled at once. She hadn't resigned. She had signed up for a weekend sound course, and she now had one honest answer instead of a daydream.

qa.q: What did Parul say was the boring part nobody mentions?
qa.a: Logging footage. Hours of it.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she read Parul's notes?
qa.a: Stung and oddly thrilled at once: the criticism hurt, but real feedback on real work excited her 😊

qa.q: Why was the trailer a wise experiment at this stage?
qa.a: It tested editing for real and brought honest feedback while she kept her bank job, so she learned without burning bridges.

qa.q: What might Parul be thinking while giving Vasudha blunt notes?
qa.a: Parul probably wants to be genuinely useful, treating Vasudha as a serious learner rather than flattering a beginner.

grounding: Illustrates small experiments over several weeks: a conversation with someone in the admired field and a practice task that gives real feedback.

passage: At the bus stand in Nabha, Madhuri waited with a bundle of stitched blouses for a shop in Patiala. Gurpreet, her school friend, came hurrying over with news: Simran from their class had bought a house in Canada. 'And us? Still here, still twenty-six,' Gurpreet groaned. Madhuri smiled. Two years ago that line would have ruined her week. Now she thought of her mother, who learnt to read at forty, and of Harbans uncle, who opened his tailoring shop at fifty. 'Simran's life is Simran's,' she said. 'Mine is slower.' In a notebook at home was a plan in three parts: this year, a second sewing machine; next year, a short design course in Patiala; after that, an apprentice. Each month she ticked what she had done, not what others had. The bus came, dusty and late. She climbed on without hurry.

qa.q: What is the first part of Madhuri's plan?
qa.a: This year, a second sewing machine.

qa.q: Why doesn't Simran's news ruin Madhuri's week now?
qa.a: She has come to accept that lives move at different speeds, remembering her mother and Harbans uncle, so she feels steady rather than behind.

qa.q: What habit keeps Madhuri measuring progress on her own terms?
qa.a: Each month she ticks off what she has done rather than what others have, which keeps her attention on her own plan.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel hearing Madhuri's calm answer?
qa.a: Gurpreet, still stung by Simran's news, may be surprised and perhaps a little comforted that Madhuri isn't worried about being behind.

grounding: Illustrates accepting an uneven, late-opening path in a small town, with a plan in years and progress judged against one's own aims.

passage: On his fourth day in Delhi, Jomon had already ridden the metro end to end twice, just to watch the stations change. He ate chole kulche from a cart outside the college gate, burned his tongue and laughed. His hostel room smelled of fresh paint; he stuck a city map on the wall and circled places with a red pen. Avni, a second-year who ran the photography club, invited him on a Sunday walk through the old city, and he said yes before she finished. Amma called every night from Kottayam. 'Are you eating? Are you sleeping?' 'Amma, everything is so busy here, I'll call tomorrow,' he said, already pulling on his shoes. Only once, lying in bed with the fan clicking, did he think of the smell of rain on their veranda, and then the club's group chat buzzed and he forgot.

qa.q: Where did Avni invite Jomon to go?
qa.a: On a Sunday walk through the old city.

qa.q: What does Jomon riding the metro end to end suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He is thrilled by everything new in the city and full of restless energy 🎉

qa.q: What could help Jomon now, while the city still feels exciting?
qa.a: Keeping a short regular call with Amma even on busy days would give him a steady link to home for when the newness wears off.

qa.q: What might Amma be feeling when Jomon rushes off the phone?
qa.a: Amma may miss him and feel a little shut out, while also being glad he sounds so happy.

grounding: Shows a new student's honeymoon days in a new city, where excitement and activity push aside a brief moment of missing home.

passage:
'Look at this!' Salma held up a paper bag of pastries. 'Forty pence each at the market. Forty!'
Elizabeth, her new flatmate, laughed from the top bunk. 'You've said that about everything today.'
'Because everything is amazing. The trams! The library has a whole floor just for maps!'
'Did you call your family?'
'Tomorrow. Tonight there's the international students' quiz. You're coming.'
'I've got seminar reading...'
'Elizabeth. Quiz. Free pizza.'
'Fine.' Elizabeth climbed down. 'Your phone's buzzing, by the way.'
Salma glanced at it: Ammi, missed call, the third one. She typed, 'All good, so busy, love you ❤️,' and pocketed it. For a second her face went still. Then she grabbed her scarf. 'Come on, we'll be late. I want to see the canal at night too.'

qa.q: How much did the pastries cost at the market?
qa.a: Forty pence each.

qa.q: What might Salma's face going still for a second suggest?
qa.a: It hints at a moment of homesickness that Salma quickly pushes aside with the rush of plans.

qa.q: What small step could help Salma keep her energy and her link to home?
qa.a: She could set a short regular time to call Ammi, so home stays close while she keeps exploring.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Salma's first days?
qa.a: Elizabeth finds Salma's excitement funny and catching, and ends up coming to the quiz.

grounding: Illustrates the excitement of first days in a new city, with a missed call from home brushed aside by a rush of activity.

passage: The notice at the Hassan college office was in Kannada, and Jaya read it three times without understanding a word. She had come from Chennai two weeks ago for her veterinary course, and every day brought a new small fight. The hostel water came for one hour at dawn. The only shop near the gate sold a curry nothing like her mother's, and the shopkeeper shrugged at her Tamil. Her scholarship form needed a stamp from the taluk office, which was open only while her classes ran. 'In Chennai I'd have finished this in an afternoon,' she muttered, sweating in the queue. Gautam, a senior from her mentor group, found her there. 'Everyone hates week two,' he said, and translated the notice for her. It was about the water timing. She laughed despite herself, then went straight back to missing her own kitchen.

qa.q: When did the hostel water come?
qa.a: For one hour at dawn.

qa.q: What does Jaya's muttering in the queue reveal about her mood?
qa.a: That she is tired and irritated, comparing every hassle unfavourably with how easy things were in Chennai.

qa.q: How does Gautam help at this stage, and what else might help?
qa.a: He normalises the frustration and translates the notice, easing one small fight; learning a few everyday Kannada phrases could ease many more 🙂

qa.q: How might Gautam see Jaya in the queue?
qa.a: Gautam likely recognises his own early weeks in her sweaty frustration and wants to make things a little easier for her.

grounding: Illustrates small frustrations of language, food, water and paperwork piling up in a new town, and the habit of comparing everything with home.

passage: Rashmi, you're leaving for Hyderabad next month, so listen to your Jeevan thatha for once. At nineteen I took the train from Mangalore to Bombay for a mill job. The first week was all noise and wonder. By the sixth week, nobody knew my name. The canteen rice was wrong, the fish was wrong, even the rain smelled wrong. I shared a room with five men from Bihar who were kind, but their jokes went over my head. At night I lay on my mat and cried into my towel so nobody would hear. I wrote to my amma that I wanted to come home. She wrote back, 'Come if you must. But wait till Deepavali first.' I waited. That crying didn't mean I had chosen wrong, kutty. It meant I loved where I came from. Both things were true.

qa.q: Where did Jeevan go at nineteen, and why?
qa.a: He took the train from Mangalore to Bombay for a mill job.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he cried into his towel?
qa.a: He was homesick and lonely, missing familiar food and being known, and felt like an outsider among kind strangers.

qa.q: What helped Jeevan through this stage?
qa.a: His amma's letter allowed him to come home but asked him to wait till Deepavali, which gave him time without shame.

qa.q: What might Jeevan's amma have felt reading his letter?
qa.a: She likely felt the ache of missing him and worry, yet chose to steady him rather than pull him straight home.

grounding: Shows homesickness and culture shock weeks after a move, with night-time crying that does not mean the move was a mistake.

passage: On Pongal night, Shankar's phone screen cracked in the tram door, and with it went his video call home. He was twenty, seven weeks into his engineering exchange in Stuttgart, and the one thing he had planned all week was watching Amma draw the kolam live. Now the screen was a black web. In the shared kitchen, his flatmate Lokesh, from Hubballi, was stirring instant noodles. 'Use my laptop,' Lokesh offered, but the Wi-Fi was down in the whole building. Shankar sat on the floor by the radiator. Nobody here knew it was a festival. Nobody knew he liked his rice with ghee. He cried quietly, and was surprised at himself. Lokesh sat down beside him with two bowls. 'Library Wi-Fi, first thing tomorrow,' he said. 'You'll see the kolam, just a day late.' Shankar nodded and ate, homesick and grateful at once.

qa.q: What ruined Shankar's plan for the video call?
qa.a: His phone screen cracked in the tram door, and the Wi-Fi was down in the whole building.

qa.q: Why was Shankar surprised at himself?
qa.a: He didn't expect to cry; the missed festival call showed how much he missed his family and being known.

qa.q: What helped at this point, and what could help next?
qa.a: Lokesh's company and the plan for library Wi-Fi eased the night; regular calls home could keep his base steady through the harder weeks.

qa.q: What might Lokesh be experiencing as he sits beside Shankar?
qa.a: Lokesh, also far from home, may recognise the feeling and want to comfort his flatmate without any fuss 🤍

grounding: Illustrates homesickness weeks into a move abroad, made sharper by a broken phone on a festival night, with crying that does not mean the move was wrong.

passage: I'm Vidya, and this is about the week my son Raghav sounded low. He had moved to Kolkata for his hotel-management course, and on Thursday his voice was flat. 'The food's fine, Amma,' he said, and it clearly wasn't. After I hung up I sat in his empty room and cried, and I wanted so badly to say, come home, we'll find a college here. My sister said I should tell him how much I was suffering. I didn't. Instead I called every evening at nine, just ten minutes, never asking when he'd be back. I told him about the neighbour's new calf and the mango pickle I was sending. By the second week he laughed at the calf story. I still miss him terribly. But I think he needed a home to lean on, not a door to walk back through.

qa.q: What time did Vidya call Raghav each evening?
qa.a: At nine, for just ten minutes.

qa.q: What did Vidya want to say after the Thursday call, and why didn't she?
qa.a: She wanted to tell him to come home because she missed him and was worried, but she held back so he could keep growing there.

qa.q: Why was Vidya's way of calling a good choice?
qa.a: Short, warm, regular calls with no guilt and no questions about returning gave Raghav a steady base while he found his feet.

qa.q: What might Raghav feel on hearing the calf story?
qa.a: Raghav may feel comforted and connected to home, able to laugh again without feeling pulled back.

grounding: Shows a parent at home feeling the child's absence and worry, and choosing warm regular calls without guilt or demands to return.

passage:
Student Wellbeing Cell, note, 14 August.
Tejas, first year, came in after his father, Mr Hrithik Joshi, phoned the hostel office twice in one day. Tejas said his father had heard him sounding low on Sunday and panicked. With Tejas's permission I spoke to Mr Joshi on speaker. He said the house had felt too quiet since Tejas left, and he had been setting three plates at dinner out of habit. He admitted he had told Tejas, 'If you're unhappy, just come back, why suffer?' and then felt guilty when Tejas went silent. We talked about calls that keep the door warm without pulling. He agreed to a fixed Sunday call and to ask about Tejas's day, not about returning. Tejas looked relieved. Next steps: emailed Mr Joshi our short guide for parents; will check in with Tejas in two weeks.

qa.q: What had Mr Joshi been doing at dinner out of habit?
qa.a: Setting three plates.

qa.q: How did Mr Joshi feel after telling Tejas to just come back?
qa.a: He felt guilty when Tejas went silent, sensing that his worry had turned into pressure.

qa.q: What change was agreed to help both of them?
qa.a: A fixed Sunday call in which Mr Joshi asks about Tejas's day rather than about returning, so Tejas keeps a base without being pulled home.

qa.q: What might Tejas have felt hearing his father say the house felt too quiet?
qa.a: Tejas may have felt touched and a little guilty, then relieved once the calls were set up without pressure to come back.

grounding: Illustrates a parent at home missing a son who sounds low, first pulling him back and then agreeing to warm, regular calls without demands.

subtype: Stage 4: Loneliness and testing the new place [Actor]
passage: Sarita, you asked how Chennai is, so here's the honest version. At the office they call me 'Vijay from Nagpur,' and they're friendly, really. Lunch together, jokes in the team chat. But at six they all go home to their people, and I go home to a fan and a phone. Saturdays are the worst. I've cleaned the flat twice by noon. So I've been trying things. I joined a Sunday running group at the beach; three weeks in, they know my name, not my life. I knocked on the neighbour's door with extra sweets from home; the aunty was kind, and now we talk on the stairs. Last week I found a Marathi mandal and went for their Ganpati practice. It's slow. I thought I'd have friends in a month. It's been four months, and I'm starting to think it's more like a year.

qa.q: Where does Vijay's running group meet?
qa.a: At the beach, on Sundays.

qa.q: What does cleaning the flat twice by noon suggest about how Vijay feels on Saturdays?
qa.a: It suggests loneliness and restlessness; the empty weekend feels long, so Vijay fills it with chores.

qa.q: Which of Vijay's efforts could help most over time, and why?
qa.a: Keeping at the running group, the neighbour and the mandal together, while accepting it takes months, gives friendships time to grow.

qa.q: What might Sarita be feeling hearing this honest version?
qa.a: Sarita may feel concern about the lonely weekends but also glad to be trusted with the truth, and hopeful seeing Vijay keep trying.

grounding: Shows loneliness in a new city where colleagues are friendly but distant, and the discovery that clubs and neighbours build friendship slowly.

subtype: Stage 4: Loneliness and testing the new place [Actor]
passage: I'm Jatin, and Amandeep joined our team in Bengaluru in March, straight from Ludhiana. She's sharp at the work and polite at lunch. But on Mondays, when we ask about weekends, she says 'relaxed' and changes the subject. Once, dropping by for a charger on a Saturday, I saw her alone in the office pantry, laptop open, no work on it, just a cooking video. In May she put up a notice in the lift for a Punjabi-speaking book circle. Two people came, she told me, laughing, and one left early. Then she tried the office badminton club. She comes on Thursdays now, not great at it, cheerful. I don't know what her weekends really feel like. I only know she keeps trying, and last Friday she asked if I wanted to join her and the book-circle guy for chole at a stall she'd found.

qa.q: What notice did Amandeep put up in the lift?
qa.a: A notice for a Punjabi-speaking book circle.

qa.q: What might Amandeep's 'relaxed' answer on Mondays suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It may cover lonely, empty weekends she doesn't want to talk about, though Jatin can't be sure.

qa.q: What is Amandeep doing well at this stage?
qa.a: She keeps testing different ways to meet people, the book circle and badminton, and starts inviting others, accepting that it builds slowly.

qa.q: How does Jatin see Amandeep's first months?
qa.a: Jatin notices signs of loneliness but admits not knowing about her weekends, and seems pleased to be invited for chole.

grounding: Illustrates, through a colleague's eyes, a newcomer's empty weekends and slow attempts through clubs and people from her region to make friends.

passage: Gargi had moved to Mumbai in January, and in the third week of March everything went wrong at once. On Monday her pitch was rejected in front of the whole client team. On Tuesday the fever started. By Wednesday night she lay in her rented room in Andheri, sheets damp, kettle empty, rain hammering on the tin sunshade. No Maa bringing rasam, no cousin two streets away. She scrolled flights home and whispered, 'What was I thinking, coming here?' Her thumb hovered over Neelam's name, the quiet designer from the next desk; they had shared lunch exactly twice. She typed, 'Sorry, bit random, I'm unwell and alone, is there a chemist that delivers?' Neelam called within minutes and arrived an hour later with soup, a thermometer and the number of a nearby clinic. 'If it doesn't settle, we'll go together,' Neelam said. Gargi cried from relief.

qa.q: What did Neelam bring?
qa.a: Soup, a thermometer and the number of a nearby clinic.

qa.q: What does Gargi scrolling flights home suggest about her state of mind?
qa.a: Her doubt about the move had peaked; ill and alone after a setback, she questioned why she had come at all.

qa.q: What turned the stretch for Gargi?
qa.a: Reaching out to Neelam, though they barely knew each other, brought care and a plan to see a doctor together if the fever did not settle.

qa.q: What might it be like for Neelam to get Gargi's message?
qa.a: Neelam may be surprised but moved to be trusted, and responds quickly, perhaps knowing how alone a new city can feel.

grounding: Shows a low point after a work setback and illness in a new city, where doubt peaks and reaching out to a colleague turns things.

passage:
'Chandu akka, don't panic, okay?' Sachin said, his face grey on the video call.
'Now I'm panicking. What happened?'
'The project I've been on since I moved here got scrapped. Four months, gone. And the landlord says the flat's being sold.'
'Oh, Sachin.'
'I don't know anyone here to even rant to. I walked around Hitech City for two hours so I wasn't just sitting in the room.'
'Have you eaten?'
'Chips.'
'Sachin.'
He laughed weakly. 'I keep thinking I should just come back to Vizag. Maybe this was a mistake.'
'Maybe. Maybe not. Don't decide in your worst week.' Chandrika pulled her laptop closer. 'Tonight, order real food. Tomorrow, call that college senior you mentioned, Ravi. And call me every evening this week, even for two minutes.'
'Every evening?'
'Every evening. I'm your net until you build one here.'

qa.q: How long did Sachin walk around Hitech City?
qa.a: For two hours.

qa.q: What is Sachin worried he got wrong at this point?
qa.a: He doubts the move itself, wondering if coming was a mistake after losing his project and his flat in the same week.

qa.q: What does Chandrika's advice get right?
qa.a: She tells him not to decide in his worst week and gives small steps: real food, a call to Ravi and a daily check-in with her.

qa.q: What is it like for Chandrika to see her brother this low?
qa.a: She is worried and briefly panicked, yet steadies herself to be his support until he builds his own 🫂

grounding: Illustrates the low point of a move, when a work setback and housing trouble without local support make doubt peak, and reaching out helps.

passage: Everyone in this office calls me Manoj bhai now, Siddharth, but when I arrived in Dubai at twenty-four, nobody called me anything. What changed it wasn't one big thing. I found a tiny Kerala tea shop near the metro and went every morning at seven, same seat. After a month the owner poured my tea before I asked. I joined the Friday cricket in the park, bad batsman, loyal fielder. I learned to say shukran properly and to wait for the call to prayer to finish before phoning clients. And every Sunday I still made my mother's sambar, even when it tasted wrong. Those small things held me up while friendships took their time. So pick your tea shop, Siddharth. Pick your Sunday dish. The rest comes.

qa.q: What did Manoj make every Sunday?
qa.a: His mother's sambar, even when it tasted wrong.

qa.q: How can you tell the tea shop made Manoj feel he belonged?
qa.a: He went every morning to the same seat and still remembers the owner pouring his tea before he asked, a sign of finally being known.

qa.q: What does Manoj advise Siddharth to do?
qa.a: Pick a regular place and keep a ritual from home, like a tea shop and a Sunday dish, so there is steadiness while friends slowly form.

qa.q: What might Siddharth take from hearing that Manoj once felt unknown too?
qa.a: Siddharth may feel less alone in the first month, seeing that even the well-known Manoj bhai started out as a stranger.

grounding: Shows building roots through a regular tea shop, a sports group, local customs and a home ritual, which give steadiness while ties form.

passage: Night shifts at the warehouse in Brampton made routines hard, and the January snow made them harder. Gurpreet, twenty-five and eight months into Canada, slept while the street was awake. Still, she had built three things. Every Tuesday, snow or not, she walked to the gurdwara for the morning langar and stayed to help wash the big steel pots. Every Thursday she met Nirmala, a retired teacher from the ground floor, at the library's conversation hour, where they swapped words: Gurpreet taught a little Punjabi, and Nirmala taught winter ones like slush, black ice and toque. And every night before her shift she braided her hair the way her bebe had taught her, humming the same old song. This week the storm closed the library. So Nirmala knocked on her door with a flask of tea instead, and they practised in the corridor.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do every Tuesday?
qa.a: She walked to the gurdwara for the morning langar and stayed to help wash the big steel pots.

qa.q: What does braiding her hair the way her bebe taught her suggest about Gurpreet?
qa.a: It suggests she draws comfort and steadiness from keeping a piece of home alive inside her new life.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet keep her routines going despite night shifts and snow?
qa.a: She tied them to fixed days rather than fixed places, so when the library closed, the practice simply moved to the corridor.

qa.q: What might the Thursday meetings mean to Nirmala?
qa.a: For Nirmala, retired and living downstairs, they may be a welcome friendship, which is why the tea arrived when the library shut 😊

grounding: Illustrates building routines and roots abroad through a community place, a new friendship and a ritual from home, despite night shifts and a snowstorm.

passage:
Last March, Tejas's first spring in Guwahati: he still called Pune 'home' and Guwahati 'here,' and counted the days until Diwali leave.
This March, a Saturday: flying back from his cousin's wedding in Pune, his suitcase heavy with bakarwadi, Tejas caught himself saying on the phone, 'I'll be home by nine,' meaning his rented flat near the Brahmaputra. He smiled at that.
Monday, two days later: Hrithik, a new hire from Jaipur, sat at the next desk looking lost. At lunch Tejas walked him to the momo stall he loved, showed him which bus avoided the Beltola jam, and said, 'The third week is rough. Message me.' That evening Tejas sent a photo of the river to his mother in Pune and a photo of her kitchen to the office group. Both places, he thought, had made him.

qa.q: What was in Tejas's suitcase when he flew back from Pune?
qa.a: Bakarwadi, from his cousin's wedding.

qa.q: Why did Tejas smile when he said 'I'll be home by nine'?
qa.a: He realised Guwahati had quietly become home too, and he felt surprised and warmed by it.

qa.q: How does Tejas use his own year to help Hrithik?
qa.a: He shares practical tips and warns that the third week is rough, inviting Hrithik to message him, which makes the start less lonely.

qa.q: What might Hrithik be feeling at lunch with Tejas?
qa.a: Hrithik, new and lost, probably feels relieved to have someone show the way and admit the hard weeks ahead.

grounding: Shows, across a year and two days, a person for whom home has become two places, who feels grateful to both and guides a newcomer.

passage: Payal, before you go, let your Indu maasi tell you one thing. When I moved to Singapore at twenty-five, I thought one day I'd have to choose, here or Kanpur. By the second year I stopped choosing. On Sunday mornings I bought kaya toast at the hawker centre with my neighbour, Mrs Tan, and on Sunday evenings I called your nani and heard every detail of the gali. I kept a jar of her aam ka achaar on my shelf and a pot of pandan on my windowsill. When a young nurse from Lucknow joined my ward and cried in the locker room in her first month, I took her to the hawker centre and told her it gets easier. It does. I'm grateful to both places, beta. Kanpur gave me my roots; Singapore gave me my spine. You'll carry two homes too, and still be only you.

qa.q: What did Indu keep on her windowsill?
qa.a: A pot of pandan.

qa.q: What does Indu mean by 'Kanpur gave me my roots; Singapore gave me my spine'?
qa.a: She feels grateful to both: Kanpur gave her family and belonging, and Singapore made her strong and independent.

qa.q: How did Indu pass on what she had learned?
qa.a: She took the crying new nurse from Lucknow to the hawker centre and reassured her, helping a newcomer through the same path.

qa.q: How might Payal feel hearing this before leaving?
qa.a: Payal may feel reassured that moving does not mean losing home, and that Indu maasi understands what lies ahead.

grounding: Illustrates a person who, after moving, holds two homes with gratitude and helps a newcomer through the same path.
